issues.legal_issue: A purchase-tax notification covering standing trees or bamboos agreed to be severed is valid when it taxes a completed purchase of goods rather than an agreement to sever.
material_facts: The challenged notifications declared standing trees and bamboos agreed to be severed liable to purchase tax.
The statutory definitions of goods included things attached to land that were agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
The notifications, read as a whole, taxed the turnover of purchases, and the purchase could be completed before severance.
issues.conclusion: The challenged notifications and entries were constitutional and valid; their subject matter was goods and the taxable event was a completed purchase, not an agreement to sever.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 54 of List II permits taxation of sales or purchases of goods, but not transactions that are not sales or purchases of goods under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Sections 3B and 5(1) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, operate on the turnover of purchases and the rate of tax. Under sections 4 and 18–23 of the Sale of Goods Act, property may pass before severance when the goods are specific or ascertained, the contract is unconditional, and the goods are in a deliverable state, unless a different intention appears. The Court relied on State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co., The Sales Tax Officer v. Budh Prakash Jai Prakash, Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd. v. D.P. Dube, K.L. Johar & Co. v. Deputy Commercial Tax Officer, Joint Commercial Tax Officer v. Young Men’s Indian Association, and State of Maharashtra v. Champalal Kishanlal Mohta.

predicates.challenge_to_purchase_tax_notification: A party challenged a government notification imposing purchase tax on a category of goods.
predicates.notification_covers_goods_agreed_to_be_s: The notification covers things attached to land that the parties have agreed will be severed.
predicates.purchase_is_completed_before_severance: The contract and circumstances make the purchase complete before the goods are severed.

issues.definition: When a challenged purchase-tax notification covers goods agreed to be severed and the purchase is complete before severance, the notification is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A forest contract that leaves title to standing trees with the seller until the trees are felled, checked, and removed does not make the buyer liable to purchase tax on standing trees agreed to be severed.
material_facts: The forest contracts were subject to conditions governing payment, the commencement of work, felling, routes of removal, inspection, and removal from the contract area.
The contractor could lose the right to trees not removed within the contract period, and forest officers controlled and supervised the operations.
The contractor acquired the trees only after felling, compliance with the contract conditions, inspection, and removal from the contract area.
issues.conclusion: The timber contracts were agreements to sell standing trees, not completed purchases of standing trees agreed to be severed; the challenged purchase-tax provisions did not apply to those transactions.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 18–23 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the passing of property depends on whether goods are specific or ascertained, whether the contract is unconditional, whether the goods are in a deliverable state, and the parties’ intention as shown by the contract, conduct, and circumstances. The Court relied on Badri Prasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh in considering when property in standing trees passes.

predicates.forest_contract_purchase_tax_dispute: The dispute concerns purchase tax claimed in connection with a contract for acquiring forest trees.
predicates.contract_conditions_prevent_immediate_fe: The buyer must satisfy contractual conditions and follow prescribed controls before felling and removing the trees.
predicates.title_passes_only_after_felling_inspecti: The parties’ arrangements provide that the buyer acquires the trees only after felling, inspection, and removal.

issues.definition: When a forest contract prevents immediate felling and removal and title passes only after those steps, purchase tax on a purchase of standing trees does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A long-term grant of the right to take growing forest produce, together with related land-use rights, is a profit a prendre and not a sale of goods, lease, or easement.
material_facts: The bamboo contract granted an exclusive right and licence to fell, cut, obtain, and remove bamboos over a lengthy period, including bamboos that would grow in the future.
The grantee received ancillary rights to use land, roads, and streams and to construct works for its operations.
The grantee had to pay a minimum royalty that did not correspond to the quantity of bamboos actually cut and removed.
The grantee had no right to exclusive possession of the contract area, and the grant was not for the beneficial enjoyment of other land belonging to it.
issues.conclusion: The bamboo contract was a grant of a profit a prendre, a benefit arising out of land and an interest in immovable property; amounts payable under it could not be taxed as a sale or purchase of goods under the Act or under the State’s power to tax goods.
issues.legal_principle: A profit a prendre is a right to take produce from another’s land and is a benefit arising out of land; under section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, it is immovable property. A profit a prendre is not an easement unless granted for the beneficial enjoyment of the grantee’s land. The Court relied on Ananda Behra v. State of Orissa, Shantabai v. State of Bombay, and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and held Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Orient Paper Mills Ltd. not to be good law.

predicates.bamboo_contract_tax_dispute: The dispute concerns tax imposed on payments under a grant relating to the taking of forest produce.
predicates.long_term_right_to_take_growing_forest_p: The grantee receives a right over an extended period to take produce that exists or will grow on the land.
predicates.ancillary_rights_to_use_land: The grant gives the grantee related rights to use land or access routes for its operations.
predicates.minimum_payment_not_tied_to_actual_quant: The grantee must pay a minimum amount that is not determined by the quantity of produce actually taken.

issues.definition: When a long-term forest-produce grant includes related land-use rights and a minimum payment unrelated to actual extraction, it is a profit a prendre and its payments are not taxable as payments for goods.

issues.legal_issue: A later notification issued in supersession of earlier notifications replaces them prospectively without extinguishing tax liability accrued while the earlier notifications operated.
material_facts: Earlier notifications imposed tax on the relevant purchases.
Later notifications stated that they were issued in supersession of previous notifications and took effect from a later date.
The tax liability in dispute accrued during the period when the earlier notifications were in force.
issues.conclusion: The later notifications repealed and replaced the earlier notifications but did not wipe out liability accrued under the earlier notifications.
issues.legal_principle: Where the enabling provisions authorize notifications from time to time, a later notification may repeal and replace an earlier one. The expression “in supersession” in this context does not retrospectively extinguish accrued liability; the later notifications operated from their stated effective date.

predicates.dispute_concerns_superseding_notificatio: The dispute concerns a later notification that replaces earlier notifications on the same subject.
predicates.earlier_notification_was_in_force_when_l: The earlier notification operated when the taxable transaction occurred and the liability accrued.
predicates.later_notification_operates_from_a_later: The later notification states an effective date after the period covered by the earlier notification.

issues.definition: When liability accrued under an earlier notification before a later replacement took effect, the accrued liability survives the replacement.

issues.legal_issue: The same goods cannot be taxed at more than one point in the same series of transactions by successive dealers when the governing single-point scheme prohibits repeat taxation.
material_facts: Sales of dressed or sized logs by the forest contractor had already been assessed to sales tax.
The timber sold to the contractor was processed into those logs.
The Court found that timber and logs were the same commercial commodity for this purpose.
issues.conclusion: The earlier sale of timber could not also be taxed where sales of the resulting logs had already been taxed in the same series of sales by successive dealers.
issues.legal_principle: The provisos to sections 3B and 8 of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, establish a single-point scheme: goods declared liable to purchase tax are not subject to tax on their sales, and the same goods are not to be taxed at more than one point in the same series of sales or purchases by successive dealers.

predicates.single_point_tax_dispute: The dispute concerns whether goods may be taxed at more than one point in a sequence of transactions.
predicates.same_commercial_goods_move_through_succe: Goods pass through successive dealers without becoming a different commercial commodity for the relevant tax analysis.
predicates.tax_has_already_been_assessed_at_one_poi: Tax has already been assessed on the goods at one point in the sequence.

issues.definition: When the same commercial goods pass through successive dealers and have already been taxed at one point, they cannot be taxed again at another point in that sequence.

issues.legal_issue: An assessment cannot be reopened to impose a higher rate after the statutory period for reopening has expired.
material_facts: The contractor’s sales of logs for the relevant period had been assessed at a lower rate than the State claimed was applicable.
The State’s proposed reassessment would have imposed the higher rate.
The statutory period for reopening the assessment had expired.
issues.conclusion: The assessment could not be reopened to reassess the sales at the higher rate after the limitation period had expired.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(8) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, allowed reopening only within the prescribed limitation period. After that period expired, the authority could not reopen the assessment to impose a higher rate.

predicates.tax_assessment_reopening_dispute: The dispute concerns an authority’s attempt to reopen a completed tax assessment.
predicates.authority_seeks_to_reassess_at_a_higher_: The authority seeks to reassess the taxpayer at a rate higher than the rate used in the original assessment.
predicates.reopening_period_has_expired: The time allowed by law to reopen the assessment has elapsed.

issues.definition: When an authority seeks a higher-rate reassessment after the reopening period has expired, the assessment cannot be reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A contract under which the purchaser performs the felling and removal of forest produce is not a works contract merely because those activities are required to obtain the produce.
material_facts: Under the timber contracts, the contractor, not the government, had to enter the forest, fell the trees, and remove them.
The bamboo contract likewise required the grantee to carry out the operations needed to obtain the bamboos.
The government did not undertake work or services for the contractor; it granted rights over the forest produce or land.
issues.conclusion: The timber contracts and the bamboo contract were not works contracts.
issues.legal_principle: A works contract is a contract for work or services in which the supply of materials or other goods is incidental. The Court relied on Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Purshottam Premji in distinguishing a works contract from a transaction in which the party paying the consideration performs the work.

predicates.forest_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a contract for obtaining forest produce is a works contract.
predicates.purchaser_performs_the_felling_or_extrac: The purchaser or grantee performs the work needed to fell, cut, or remove the forest produce.
predicates.grantor_does_not_undertake_work_or_servi: The grantor does not undertake work or services for the purchaser or grantee.

issues.definition: When the purchaser performs the extraction work and the grantor undertakes no work or services, the forest contract is not a works contract.

issues.legal_issue: When a term is not statutorily defined or judicially interpreted and the record does not establish its commercial meaning, its meaning may be determined from common parlance using contextual dictionary assistance.
material_facts: The Orissa Sales Tax Act did not define “timber” or “logs.”
The parties produced insufficient material to establish the terms’ meaning in commercial parlance.
The Court considered statutory definitions, dictionaries, and the context in which the terms were used.
issues.conclusion: Timber included logs and also included beams, rafters, and planks; timber and sized or dressed logs were the same commercial commodity for the issue before the Court.
issues.legal_principle: A dictionary should not displace an applicable statutory definition or judicial interpretation. In their absence, and where evidence of common usage is insufficient, a court may consult dictionaries to identify common parlance, selecting the meaning that fits the context. The Court approved Mohanlal Vishram v. Commissioner of Sales Tax and G. Ramaswamy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and overruled Krupasindhu Sahu & Sons v. State of Orissa on the relevant point.

predicates.term_interpretation_dispute: The dispute requires the court to determine the meaning of a term used to describe goods.
predicates.term_has_no_applicable_statutory_or_judi: No relevant statute or judicial decision defines or interprets the term.
predicates.commercial_usage_evidence_is_insufficien: The record does not adequately establish how the term is used in commercial or trade parlance.

issues.definition: When a disputed term lacks an applicable legal definition and commercial evidence is insufficient, its meaning may be determined from contextual common parlance.

issues.legal_issue: A document must be interpreted as a whole, and its nature cannot be determined selectively to fit a particular statute or by looking only at its end result.
material_facts: The contracts contained multiple rights, duties, payment arrangements, restrictions, and conditions relevant to their legal character.
The High Court and the earlier decision in Orient Paper Mills had focused on selected terms or on the result that produce would be severed and become movable goods.
The Court found that this approach disregarded other terms and the principle that the agreement and the eventual sale must relate to the same subject matter.
issues.conclusion: The contract’s nature had to be determined from all its terms and the rights and consequences flowing from it; the selective, end-result approach in Orient Paper Mills was wrong in law.
issues.legal_principle: A written instrument must be construed as a whole, giving effect, so far as possible, to all its clauses. The nature of a transaction cannot be made to vary according to the statute under consideration or be determined only from its eventual consequence. State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. and Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Purshottam Premji support the requirement that the agreement and the sale relate to the same subject matter. The Court rejected the contrary interpretive approach in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Orient Paper Mills Ltd.

predicates.court_must_characterize_written_contract: The court must determine the legal nature of a transaction from a written contract.
predicates.contract_contains_multiple_interrelated_: The contract includes several related terms governing rights, obligations, conditions, and consequences.

issues.definition: When a written contract has interrelated terms and must be legally characterized, the contract must be interpreted as a whole.

issues.legal_issue: When decisions of the Supreme Court conflict on the same point, a larger bench’s view is to be followed in preference to a smaller bench’s view.
material_facts: The parties relied on Supreme Court decisions expressing different views on the legal character of grants relating to forest produce.
The Court identified relevant decisions of larger benches and a contrary decision of a smaller bench.
issues.conclusion: The larger-bench decisions governed, and the contrary smaller-bench approach could not be preferred.
issues.legal_principle: The rule stated in Union of India v. K.S. Subramanian is that a court should identify and follow the view expressed by a larger bench in preference to a conflicting view expressed by a smaller bench; the practice has crystallized into a rule of law.

predicates.court_faces_conflicting_supreme_court_de: A court encounters Supreme Court decisions that express conflicting views on the same legal point.
predicates.conflicting_decisions_are_of_different_b: The conflicting decisions were delivered by benches of different sizes.

issues.definition: When Supreme Court decisions conflict and their benches differ in size, the view of the larger bench must be followed.
